gist: Before Pilate, Jesus says his reign does not originate here; were it otherwise, his people would take up arms to stop his arrest.
Sensing the crowd means to seize him and crown him by force, Jesus slips away alone into the hills.
Jesus orders Peter to sheathe his blade: the cup his Father hands him is to be drunk, not fought off.
Jesus reminds them he could summon over twelve legions of angels at once. He does not.
"Enough," he says, and restores the wounded slave's ear with a touch.
From a high peak the devil displays every realm on earth and all their glory.
The price of them all: kneel and worship the tempter.
The devil claims the authority and splendour of the realms were handed to him, to give to whoever he likes.
Jesus tells Pilate that his power over him exists only because it was granted from above.
The soldiers dress him in purple and press a crown woven of thorns onto his head.
Pilate's placard on the cross names him as Jesus of Nazareth and King of the Jews.
Jesus Christ, the trustworthy witness and first raised from death, is named ruler over earth's kings.
An elder announces that the Lion of Judah's tribe has won the victory and may open the scroll.
What John then sees is not a lion but a Lamb, standing, bearing the marks of slaughter.
As the arrest begins, his companions ask whether they should strike with their swords.
Cain lures Abel out into the open country and kills him there.
God tells Cain that the ground itself cries out to him with his brother's blood.
Lamech boasts to his wives that he killed a man, a youth, for striking and wounding him.
Cain's sevenfold vengeance becomes Lamech's seventy-seven.
Before the flood, the earth is ruined in God's eyes and full of violence.
After the flood: shed a human's blood and a human will shed yours, because humankind bears God's image.
Nimrod, Cush's son, is the earliest man the text calls a mighty warrior.
At Babel people resolve to raise a city with a tower into the sky, to make a name and not be scattered.
Bloodshed defiles the land, and only the killer's own blood can atone for it.
Jesus answers Peter: forgive not seven times, but seventy-seven.
Jesus charges that all the innocent blood ever spilled, from Abel's to Zechariah's, will come upon that generation.
The sprinkled blood of Jesus speaks something better than Abel's did.
Quarrels and fights among believers come from desires waging war inside them.
Wanting and not getting, people kill; coveting and not obtaining, they fight.
Jacob names Simeon and Levi as brothers whose swords are instruments of violence.
Gideon refuses the crown for himself and his son: the LORD is to rule Israel.
In Jotham's fable the trees set out to crown a king for themselves, and ask the olive first.
The bramble accepts: shelter in my shade, or fire will come out of me and burn the cedars.
The book closes: Israel had no king, and each did what seemed right to himself.
The elders ask Samuel to give them a king to govern them, as the nations have.
God tells Samuel the people are rejecting not him but God as their king.
They want to be like the nations, with a king who leads them out and fights their wars.
God says Israel set up kings and princes he never chose and never knew of.
The king must not build up horses for himself or send the people back to Egypt for them.
Once enthroned, the king is to have his own copy of the law written out before the priests.
So that he does not raise himself above his kin, or stray from the command.
Samuel tells Saul that God wants obedience more than burnt offerings.
Pharaoh orders the Hebrew midwives to kill newborn boys and spare girls.
Pharaoh then commands all his people to throw every Hebrew boy into the Nile.
Pharaoh asks who this LORD is that he should obey him, and refuses to release Israel.
Nebuchadnezzar's decree: anyone who will not bow to the statue goes straight into the furnace.
The officials press Darius to forbid, for thirty days, any prayer except to the king, on pain of the lions.
Letters go out across the empire ordering the Jews destroyed and their goods seized, on one appointed day.
The king explains that an order written in his name and sealed with his ring cannot be revoked.
Herod, enraged at being outwitted, has every boy two and under in and around Bethlehem killed.
Woe to those who issue unjust decrees and write statutes that oppress.
Their laws deny the poor their rights and turn widows and orphans into plunder.
Jezebel taunts Ahab about whether he truly rules Israel and promises to get him Naboth's vineyard.
In spring, the season for kings to make war, David sends Joab to ravage Ammon, and stays home.
Joshua has his commanders plant their feet on five captured kings' necks.
Adoni-bezek, maimed as he had maimed seventy kings, admits God has repaid him in kind.
Elisha weeps, foreseeing Hazael burning forts, killing young men, smashing children and ripping open pregnant women.
Ammon is condemned for slitting open Gilead's pregnant women to widen its borders.
Assyria's king credits his own strength and cleverness for erasing borders, looting treasure and toppling thrones.
In besieged Samaria a woman brings the king her complaint: a pact to eat their sons, one each day.
She cooked her son; the next day the other mother hid hers.
The covenant curse foretells it: under siege, parents will eat their own children.
In Jerusalem's fall, tender-hearted mothers boiled their children for food.
Before attacking a town, Israel must first offer it peace.
In a long siege the fruit trees are not to be cut down: a tree is not an enemy.
Achan confesses he saw a robe, silver and gold among the spoil, wanted them, took them and buried them.
Saul spares King Agag and keeps the choicest livestock and valuables instead of destroying all of it.
Abram will not take even a thread or a strap of a shoe from the king of Sodom's spoils.
Nineveh, city of blood and lies, endlessly stuffed with plunder.
Charging cavalry, flashing blades, and corpses past counting that men trip over.
Bodies will lie across the fields like dung, like sheaves left behind that no one gathers.
Ezekiel is led around a valley of bones, very many and very dry.
He is told to summon breath from the four winds into the slain so that they live.
Babylon kills Zedekiah's sons in front of him, blinds him, and carries him off in chains.
The Chaldeans sweep through like wind; their own strength is their god.
A red horse's rider is permitted to strip the earth of peace, so people slaughter each other; he is handed a great sword.
An angel stationed in the sun summons every bird in mid-heaven to God's great supper.
The menu is the flesh of kings, commanders, the mighty, horses and riders, slave and free.
Birds and beasts are invited to eat warriors' flesh and drink the princes' blood.
Nathan charges David with killing Uriah by the Ammonite sword and taking his wife.
Therefore the sword will never leave David's house.
David is barred from building God's house because he shed much blood and fought great wars.
Where the dogs lapped Naboth's blood, they will lap Ahab's.
Whoever kills by the sword will be killed by it: a summons to the saints' endurance and faith.
Abner calls to Joab: must the sword devour forever? Kin chasing kin ends in bitterness.
Fallen Babylon is found holding the prophets' and saints' blood, and that of everyone slaughtered on earth.
The woman is drunk on the saints' blood and the blood of Jesus' witnesses.
Some boast of chariots and horses; the psalmist boasts in the name of God.
No king is rescued by the size of his army, nor a warrior by his own strength.
A warhorse is a false hope; for all its power it saves no one.
Woe to those who run to Egypt for horses and chariots and never seek the Holy One.
God will save Judah himself, not by bow, sword, battle or cavalry.
Ready the horse for battle; the victory is the LORD's.
David tells Goliath that God saves without sword or spear, for the fight belongs to the LORD.
Judah need not fear the vast army: the fight is God's, not theirs.
To Zerubbabel: not by strength, not by force, but through my spirit.
At the sea: God will do the fighting, and Israel need only be still.
After the crossing, Israel sings of the LORD as a man of war.
David blesses God for training his hands and fingers for battle.
God's sword is against Babylon's horses, chariots, hired troops and treasure.
The watchers' decree: the Most High rules over human kingdoms and gives them to whom he wills, even the lowliest.
Nebuchadnezzar admires the Babylon he built by his own might for his own glory.
Tekel: Belshazzar is weighed, and found too light.
God gives the lands to Nebuchadnezzar, calling him my servant.
God calls Cyrus his anointed, whose hand he holds to bring nations down before him.
Wisdom says it is through her that kings hold their thrones and rulers make just laws.
In one night the LORD's angel kills 185,000 in Assyria's camp.
Herod, taking glory that was God's, is struck down by an angel and eaten by worms.
Mary sings that God pulls rulers off their thrones and raises the low.
Earth's kings and rulers band together to oppose God and the one he anointed.
The one enthroned in heaven laughs at them and holds them in scorn.
The anointed will smash them with an iron rod like pottery.
So the kings are told: be wise, and take warning.
The believers apply Psalm 2 to the plot against Jesus.
The Day Star who brought the nations down is himself felled to the earth.
He had vowed to climb to heaven and set his throne above God's stars.
Onlookers stare and ask whether this is really the one who made kingdoms shake.
Kings, generals, the wealthy and the mighty hide in caves among the rocks.
The Teacher sees oppression everywhere: the oppressed weeping with no comforter, and power on the oppressors' side.
Do not be surprised by injustice in a province: every official has a higher one watching him, and those have higher still.
He observes how one person wields power over another to that person's harm.
Rulers who hate good and love evil strip the skin and flesh from God's people.
They devour them, break their bones, and cut them into pieces for the pot.
The shepherds neither healed the sick nor sought the lost, but ruled with force and harshness.
Jerusalem's officials are wolves tearing prey, shedding blood for profit.
To the poor, a wicked ruler is a lion that roars or a bear on the charge.
The people rejoice under the righteous and groan under the wicked.
Do justice, rescue the robbed from the oppressor, do no violence to alien, orphan or widow, shed no innocent blood.
What God asks of a person: do justice, love kindness, walk humbly with him.
The prayer for the king: may he defend the poor and crush the oppressor.
John tells soldiers not to extort by threats or false charges, and to be content with their pay.
A king is promised who reigns in righteousness and princes who rule with justice.
Jesus: the rulers of the nations lord it over their people and their great men tyrannise them.
Not among you: here, greatness means being a servant.
He came to serve, not be served, and to lay down his life as a ransom for many.
Mark's form: those reckoned to rule the nations lord it over them.
Luke's form: the kings of the nations dominate them and are hailed as benefactors.
The greatest must be like the youngest, the leader like a servant.
He emptied himself, took a slave's form, and was born as a human.
He lowered himself and obeyed all the way to dying on a cross.
The servant will not shout or raise his voice in the street.
He will not break a bruised reed or snuff out a faint wick, yet he brings justice.
Zion's king arrives victorious, yet humble, riding a donkey's colt.
He removes chariot, warhorse and bow, and speaks peace to the nations.
Matthew cites Zechariah as Jesus rides into Jerusalem.
Oppressed and afflicted, he stayed silent, a lamb led to slaughter.
The law of like for like: eye, tooth, hand, foot.
No revenge and no grudge against your own people; love your neighbour as yourself.
God claims vengeance and repayment as his own.
Jesus recalls the old saying about an eye for an eye.
He says not to resist the one who does evil: struck on one cheek, offer the other.
Love those who are your enemies, and pray on behalf of your persecutors.
Paul: repay no one evil for evil.
Never take revenge; leave room for God's wrath, since Scripture says repayment is his.
Conquer evil with good, rather than be conquered by it.
Insulted, Christ did not insult back; suffering, he made no threats, but trusted the just judge.
On the cross Jesus asks the Father to forgive them, since they are unaware of what they do.
Stephen, dying under the stones, asks the Lord not to charge this sin to them.
James and John offer to call fire from heaven down on a Samaritan village.
Jesus turns and rebukes them.
Elisha refuses to let the king kill the captured Arameans: feed them and send them home.
After a great feast they go home, and the raiding bands stop coming.
David will not lift his hand against Saul, the LORD's anointed.
Joseph tells his brothers: you meant me harm, God meant it for good.
God will judge the nations; swords become plowshares, spears pruning hooks, and war is no longer learned.
Micah gives the same vision of nations disarmed by God's judgement.
The call reversed: hammer plowshares into swords, and let the weak claim to be a warrior.
God ends wars to the ends of the earth, breaking bow and spear and burning shields.
God will banish bow, sword and warfare from the land, and let his people rest in safety.
A child is born who bears authority on his shoulders, named Prince of Peace.
His rule and peace will grow without end, upheld by justice.
There God broke the arrows, the shield and the blade.
Wars and rumours of wars will come; do not be alarmed, for that is not yet the end.
There is a season for war and a season for peace.
The patient outdo the mighty, and self-control beats taking a city.
Wisdom beats weapons, yet one fool undoes much good.
A poor wise man saved the city, and no one remembered him.
Everyone should submit to the governing authorities, since none exists apart from God.
The ruler is God's servant for good and carries the sword for a reason, executing wrath on wrongdoers.
Peter and the apostles: God must be obeyed over any human authority.
Peter and John ask the council to judge for itself whether heeding it over God is right.
Pilate reminds the silent Jesus that he holds power to free him or crucify him.
The midwives fear God, disobey Pharaoh, and let the boys live.
The three tell the king their God is able to save them from the furnace.
And even if he does not, they will not serve his gods or bow to his statue.
Pray for kings and all in high office, so that life may be quiet and peaceful.
The chief priests declare that the emperor is their only king.
Gamaliel, a respected teacher of the law, has the apostles taken out for a moment.
Theudas rose up with about four hundred men; he was killed, and his followers scattered.
Judas of Galilee rose up in the census days; he died, and his followers dispersed.
Gamaliel: leave these men alone, for a plan of human origin will collapse.
If it is from God you cannot overthrow it, and you may find yourselves fighting God.
A stone cut without hands strikes the statue's iron-and-clay feet and shatters them.
God will establish a kingdom that is never destroyed, and it will end all the others.
The one like a son of man receives an everlasting dominion that will not pass.
The LORD brings the nations' counsel to nothing and frustrates the plans of peoples.
His counsel stands forever, his purposes for every generation.
People make many plans, but God's purpose is what stands.
No wisdom or counsel succeeds against the LORD.
God has planned it: who can annul it, or turn back his hand?
Jesus: the time has come to its fullness, and God's kingdom has come near.
When time reached its fullness, God sent his Son.
The vision awaits its appointed time; if it is slow, wait, for it will surely come.
The least will become a nation; in its time, God says, he will hasten it.
The world's kingdom becomes the kingdom of the Lord and his Messiah, who reigns forever.
The struggle is not with flesh and blood, but with rulers, authorities and cosmic powers.
The weapons of this warfare are more than human, and they tear down strongholds.
Christ disarmed the rulers and powers and paraded them in his triumph.
Had this age's rulers understood, they would never have crucified the glorious Lord.
At the end he hands the kingdom to the Father, having abolished every ruler and power.
They conquered the accuser by the Lamb's blood and their testimony, not clinging to life.
Kings wage war against the Lamb, and he conquers them, being King of kings.
The beast and earth's kings gather their armies against the rider and his army.
Asked when the kingdom comes: it does not come in a way that can be watched for.
No one will say look here or there, for it is among you.
Since John the Baptist, the kingdom suffers violence, and the violent try to seize it.
